references.text: The charges against Jesus that Pilate refers to: the Jewish leaders had accused him of misleading the people, preventing payment of taxes to Caesar, and calling himself Christ, a king ([ref:Luk 23:2|Luke 23:2]).
Pilate had already declared once that he found no guilt in Jesus ([ref:Luk 23:4|Luke 23:4]). In verse 14, he repeats this after questioning him more thoroughly.
For the third time, Pilate declares Jesus' innocence and says he has found nothing in him deserving of death ([ref:Luk 23:22|Luke 23:22]).
Also in the Gospel of John, Pilate declares that he finds no guilt in Jesus ([ref:Joh 18:38|John 18:38]), which aligns with Pilate's statement in Luke 23:14.
Pilate repeats to the crowd that he finds no guilt in Jesus ([ref:Joh 19:4|John 19:4]), paralleling his repeated declarations of innocence in Luke.
Once again, Pilate says he finds no fault in Jesus ([ref:Joh 19:6|John 19:6]), consistent with Luke's portrayal of Pilate as one who repeatedly clears Jesus.
Matthew reports that Pilate washed his hands and declared himself innocent of Jesus' blood, because he found no basis to condemn him ([ref:Matt 27:23-24|Matthew 27:23-24]).
Also in Mark, Pilate asks the crowd what evil Jesus has done, thereby implying that he found no guilt ([ref:Mark 15:14|Mark 15:14]).
Paul preached that although they found no ground for death against Jesus, they asked Pilate to have him executed ([ref:Apg 13:28|Acts 13:28]), a direct parallel to Pilate's finding in Luke 23:14.

The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant says he had done no wrong and that no deceit was found in his mouth ([ref:Jes 53:9|Isaiah 53:9]), which is confirmed by Pilate's judgment that Jesus was innocent.
Peter confirms that Christ had committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth ([ref:1 Pet 2:22|1 Peter 2:22]), in agreement with Pilate's declaration of Jesus' innocence.
